danish.title: Fjortende bog (1812) — Kapitel 13
paragraphs: Midt på dagen den 22. oktober gik Pierre opad den mudrede, glatte vej og kiggede på sine fødder og vejens ujævnheder. Nu og da kastede han et blik på den velkendte flok omkring sig og derefter igen på sine fødder. Begge dele var lige velkendte og hans egne. Den gråblå, hjulbenede hund løb muntert langs vejsiden, af og til løftede den som bevis på sin smidighed og selvtilfredshed det ene bagben og hoppede af sted på tre, og så gik den igen på alle fire og styrtede hen for at gø ad kragerne, der sad på de døde kroppe. Hunden var muntrere og mere velnæret end i Moskva. Rundt omkring lå kød af forskellige dyr — fra mennesker til heste — i forskellige stadier af opløsning; og da ulvene blev holdt borte af de forbimarcherende, kunne hunden æde alt, hvad den havde lyst til.

Det havde regnet siden morgenstunden og havde hele tiden set ud, som om det hvert øjeblik kunne holde op og himlen klare op, men efter en kort pause begyndte det at regne hårdere end før. Den gennemblødte vej absorberede ikke længere vandet, som løb i strømme i hjulsporene.
Pierre gik af sted, kiggede til begge sider, talte sine skridt i grupper af tre og regnede dem af på fingrene. Han henvendte sig mentalt til regnen og gentog: »Nå så, nå så, fortsæt! Styrk hårdere!«

Det forekom ham, at han ikke tænkte på noget, men langt nede og dybt i sit indre var hans sjæl optaget af noget vigtigt og trøstende. Dette noget var en yderst fin åndelig slutning udledt af en samtale med Karatajev dagen forinden.

Ved gårsdagens rasteplads, hvor Pierre frøs ved et døende lejrbål, var han stået op og gået hen til det næste, som brændte bedre. Der sad Platon Karatajev indhyllet — med hoved og det hele — i sin kappe, som var det en messehagel, og fortalte soldaterne med sin virkningsfulde og behagelige, omend nu svage stemme, en historie, Pierre kendte. Det var allerede over midnat, den time hvor Karatajev sædvanligvis var fri for sin feber og særlig livlig. Da Pierre nåede hen til bålet og hørte Platons stemme, svækket af sygdom, og så hans ynkelige ansigt stærkt oplyst af flammerne, følte han et smertefuldt stik i hjertet. Hans følelse af medynk med denne mand skræmte ham, og han ville gerne gå sin vej, men der var ikke noget andet bål, og Pierre satte sig ned og prøvede at lade være med at se på Platon.
»Nå, hvordan har du det?« spurgte han.
»Hvordan har jeg det? Hvis vi brokker os over sygdom, skænker Gud os ikke døden,« svarede Platon og genoptog straks den historie, han var begyndt på.
»Og så, bror,« fortsatte han med et smil på sit blege, udmagrede ansigt og et særligt lykkeligt lys i øjnene, »ser du, bror...«

Pierre havde længe kendt den historie. Karatajev havde fortalt ham den alene en fem-seks gange og altid med en særlig glad bevægelse i stemmen. Men skønt han kendte den godt, lyttede Pierre nu til den historie, som var den noget nyt, og den stille henrykkelse, Karatajev tydeligvis følte, da han fortalte den, meddelte sig også til Pierre. Historien handlede om en gammel købmand, der levede et godt og gudfrygtigt liv med sin familie, og som engang drog til markedet i Nizjnij med en ledsager — en rig købmand.

Da de havde taget ind på et værtshus, lagde de sig begge til at sove, og næste morgen blev ledsageren fundet berøvet og med overskåret strube. En blodig kniv blev fundet under den gamle købmands hovedpude. Han blev stillet for retten, pisket med knuten, og efter at hans næsefløje var revet af, »alt efter forskrifterne«, som Karatajev udtrykte det, blev han sendt til straffearbejde i Sibirien.

»Og så, bror« (det var på dette sted, Pierre var kommet hen), »gik der ti år eller mere. Den gamle mand levede som straffefange, fandt sig i alt, som han skulle, og gjorde intet ondt. Han bad blot Gud om døden. Nå, en nat var fangerne samlet ligesom vi, med den gamle mand iblandt dem. Og de begyndte at fortælle, hvad hver især var straffet for, og hvordan de havde syndet mod Gud. Den ene fortalte, at han havde taget et liv, en anden havde taget to, en tredje havde sat ild til et hus, mens en fjerde bare havde været vagabond og ikke gjort noget. Så spurgte de den gamle mand: 'Hvad bliver du straffet for, fader?' — 'Jeg, mine kære brødre,' sagde han, 'straffes for mine egne og andres synder. Men jeg har ikke slået nogen ihjel eller taget noget, der ikke var mit, men har kun hjulpet mine fattige brødre. Jeg var købmand, mine kære brødre, og havde stor rigdom.' Og han fortalte dem det hele i rette orden. 'Jeg sørger ikke for min egen skyld,' siger han, 'men Gud har tilsyneladende tugtet mig. Kun er jeg ked af det for min gamle kone og børnene,' og den gamle mand begyndte at græde. Nu skete det, at i den gruppe var netop den mand, der havde slået den anden købmand ihjel. 'Hvor skete det, fader?' sagde han. 'Hvornår, og i hvilken måned?' Han spurgte om alting, og hans hjerte begyndte at gøre ondt. Så kommer han hen til den gamle mand sådan her og falder ned for hans fødder! 'Du lider på grund af mig, fader,' siger han. 'Det er den rene sandhed, drenge, at denne mand,' siger han, 'pines uskyldig og for ingenting! Jeg,' siger han, 'begik den gerning, og jeg lagde kniven under dit hovedgærde, mens du sov. Tilgiv mig, fader,' siger han, 'for Kristi skyld!'«
Karatajev holdt inde, smilede lykkeligt mens han stirrede ind i ilden, og lagde brænderne bedre sammen.

»Og den gamle mand sagde: 'Gud vil tilgive dig, vi er alle syndere i hans øjne. Jeg lider for mine egne synder,' og han græd bitre tårer. Nå, og hvad tror I så, kære venner?« fortsatte Karatajev, mens hans ansigt lyste mere og mere op af et henrykket smil, som om det, han nu skulle fortælle, rummede historiens største charme og hele mening: »Hvad tror I, kære venner? Den morder tilstod over for myndighederne. 'Jeg har taget seks liv,' sagde han (han var en stor synder), 'men det, der plager mig mest, er denne gamle mand. Lad ham ikke lide for min skyld.' Så han tilstod, og det blev alt sammen skrevet ned og papirerne sendt af sted i rette form. Stedet var langt borte, og mens de dømte — med ét og andet, papirerne udfyldt efter alle forskrifter — myndighederne altså — gik tiden. Sagen nåede tsaren. Omsider kom tsarens dekret: at sætte købmanden fri og give ham den erstatning, der var tilkendt. Papiret ankom, og de begyndte at lede efter den gamle mand. 'Hvor er den gamle mand, der har lidt uskyldig og forgæves? Et papir er kommet fra tsaren!' Så de begyndte at lede efter ham,« her skælvede Karatajevs underkæbe, »men Gud havde allerede tilgivet ham — han var død! Sådan var det, kære venner!« sluttede Karatajev og sad længe tavs, stirrende frem for sig med et smil.

Og Pierres sjæl fyldtes dunkelt men lykkeligt, ikke af selve historien, men af dens mystiske betydning: af den henrykte glæde, der lyste i Karatajevs ansigt, da han fortalte den, og af denne glædes mystiske mening.

english.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: At midday on October twenty-second, Pierre was trudging uphill along the muddy, slippery road, looking at his feet and at the roughness of the way. Occasionally he glanced at the familiar crowd around him, then back at his feet again. Both were equally familiar and felt like part of himself. The blue-gray, bandy-legged dog ran merrily alongside the road, sometimes lifting one hind leg to hop along on three as proof of its agility and good spirits, then going on all four again and rushing off to bark at crows sitting on carrion. The dog was merrier and sleeker than it had been in Moscow. All around lay the flesh of different creatures—from humans to horses—in various stages of decay; and since wolves were kept away by the passing men, the dog could eat all it wanted.

It had been raining since morning, seeming as though it might stop any minute and the sky clear, but after a brief pause it rained harder than before. The saturated road no longer absorbed the water, which ran along the ruts in streams.
Pierre walked along looking from side to side, counting his steps in threes and ticking them off on his fingers. Mentally addressing the rain, he repeated: "Come on now, come on! Pour harder!"

He seemed to be thinking of nothing, but deep down inside him, his soul was occupied with something important and comforting. This something was a very subtle spiritual insight drawn from a conversation with Karataev the day before.

At their previous stopping place, feeling chilled by a dying campfire, Pierre had gotten up and gone to the next one, which was burning better. There Platon Karataev sat covered up—head and all—with his greatcoat as if it were a vestment, telling the soldiers in his warm and pleasant, though now weakened voice, a story Pierre already knew. It was past midnight, the hour when Karataev was usually free of his fever and especially lively. When Pierre reached the fire and heard Platon's voice, weakened by illness, and saw his thin face brightly lit by the blaze, he felt a painful stab in his heart. His feeling of pity for this man frightened him, and he wanted to leave, but there was no other fire, so Pierre sat down, trying not to look at Platon.
"Well, how are you?" he asked.
"How am I? If we complain about sickness, God won't grant us death," replied Platon, and immediately resumed the story he had begun.
"And so, brother," he continued, with a smile on his pale, wasted face and a particularly joyful light in his eyes, "you see, brother..."

Pierre had long been familiar with that story. Karataev had told it to him alone some half-dozen times, always with a special joyful emotion. But though he knew it well, Pierre now listened as though it were something new, and the quiet rapture Karataev clearly felt as he told it communicated itself to Pierre as well. The story was about an old merchant who lived a good and God-fearing life with his family, and who once went to the Nizhni fair with a companion—a rich merchant.

Having checked into an inn, they both went to sleep, and the next morning the companion was found robbed and with his throat cut. A blood-stained knife was found under the old merchant's pillow. He was tried, flogged, and his nostrils torn off, "all in proper form" as Karataev put it, and he was sent to hard labor in Siberia.

"And so, brother" (it was at this point that Pierre had come up), "ten years or more passed. The old man was living as a convict, accepting his lot as he should and doing no wrong. He only prayed to God for death. Well, one night the convicts were gathered together just as we are, with the old man among them. And they began telling what each was being punished for and how they had sinned against God. One told how he had taken a life, another had taken two, a third had set a house on fire, while another had simply been a vagrant and done nothing wrong. So they asked the old man: 'What are you being punished for, old father?' 'I, my dear brothers,' said he, 'am being punished for my own and other men's sins. But I have not killed anyone or taken anything that was not mine—I have only helped my poorer brothers. I was a merchant, dear brothers, and had much property.' And he went on to tell them everything in proper order. 'I don't grieve for myself,' he says, 'God, it seems, has chosen to punish me. Only I am sorry for my old wife and the children,' and the old man began to weep. Now it happened that in the group was the very man who had killed the other merchant. 'Where did it happen, old father?' he said. 'When, and in what month?' He asked about everything, and his heart began to ache. So he came up to the old man like this, and fell down at his feet! 'You are suffering because of me, old father,' he says. 'It's the absolute truth, lads, that this man,' he says, 'is being tortured innocently and for nothing! I,' he says, 'did that deed, and I slipped the knife under your head while you were asleep. Forgive me, old father,' he says, 'for Christ's sake!'"
Karataev paused, smiling joyfully as he gazed into the fire, and pushed the logs together.

"And the old man said, 'God will forgive you—we are all sinners in His sight. I suffer for my own sins,' and he wept bitter tears. Well, and what do you think, dear friends?" Karataev continued, his face brightening more and more with a radiant smile, as if what he was about to say contained the chief beauty and the whole meaning of his story: "What do you think, dear fellows? That murderer confessed to the authorities. 'I have taken six lives,' he says (he was a great sinner), 'but what I am most sorry for is this old man. Don't let him suffer because of me.' So he confessed, and it was all written down, and the papers were sent off in proper form. The place was far away, and while they were processing things, what with one thing and another, filling in all the papers in proper form—the authorities, I mean—time passed. The case reached the Tsar. Eventually the Tsar's decree came: to set the merchant free and give him the compensation that had been awarded. The paper arrived and they began looking for the old man. 'Where is the old man who has been suffering innocently?' A paper has come from the Tsar!' So they began looking for him," here Karataev's lower jaw trembled, "but God had already forgiven him—he was dead! That's how it was, dear fellows!" Karataev concluded, and sat for a long time in silence, gazing before him with a smile.

And Pierre's soul was dimly but joyfully filled—not by the story itself, but by its mysterious meaning: by the radiant joy that lit up Karataev's face as he told it, and by the profound significance of that joy.
